74	### Before each implementation: sync with main
75	
76	Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

78	```bash

92	Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. Never merge another

96	
97	A PR is merged with a merge commit once it is approved, every review comment is addressed and CI

116	```markdown

122	
123	## Acceptance Criteria
124	- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
125	- [ ] AC2: ...

127

129	- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>
130	
131	## Open Questions
132	- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>
133	
134	## Design Decision
135	**Decision:** <what was chosen>
136	**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
137	**Rationale:** <why this one>
138	**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>
139

166	
167	Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.

169	
170	1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
171	2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
172	3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
173	4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any

217	## UML diagrams (D6)
218	
219	The person who resolved a medium issue draws a class diagram and a sequence diagram for it. Several
220	small issues that together equal one medium issue are drawn together instead. Files:
221	
222	- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>-class.png` (or `.pdf`)
223	- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>-sequence.png` (or `.pdf`)
224	- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>.md`, which embeds both and answers the Q&A
225	
226	What the diagrams need:
227	
228	- Show the existing code found during concept location and impact analysis, and the new or changed
229	  code, and tell the two apart with a legend, colour or label.
230	- Show only the fields and methods that matter to the issue.
231	- Annotate the diagrams with the key design decisions and calls. Diagrams without annotations lose
232	  points.
233	- Add a short note on how Go maps to UML: structs, interfaces, and embedding.
234	- The `.md` follows the course template: `# Issue #<N> -- <title>`, `## Class Diagram`,
235	  `## Sequence Diagram`, `## Q&A`, each diagram embedded with
236	  `![Class diagram](<issue#>-<github-username>-class.png)` under its heading. The Q&A has 3
237	  class-diagram questions, 3 sequence-diagram questions and 1 question on AI use, answered "N/A" if
238	  no AI was used. The questions, copied from the Sprint 2 page:
239	
240	```markdown
241	**Class diagram:**
242	
243	1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.
244	2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.
245	3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?
246	
247	**Sequence diagram:**
248	
249	1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?
250	2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.
251	3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?
252	
253	**Cross-cutting:**
254	
255	4. If you used AI to create or check any part of the diagrams, describe what it produced, what you verified against the actual code, and what you had to correct or add. If AI was not used, write "N/A."
256	```
257	
258	Grading (15 points): existing code 2, solution code 2, annotations 3, UML notation (relationships,
259	cardinality, lifelines; minor errors are fine) 2, Q&A 4, AI transparency 2. The Q&A points are for
260	understanding that goes beyond what the diagram already shows, so answer with reasons, not a
261	re-description of the boxes.
262

=== #52 Sort notifications by reason or type | author: CarsonRackley | milestone:  | comments: 0
Part of #7. Related: #50 (filter by repository and type), #51 (bulk actions).

> **Stretch goal for Sprint 1.** Taken on only if #50 and #51 are done with time to spare; otherwise it carries over to Sprint 2. The spec below is a skeleton, to be filled in before implementation.

### User Story

As a user with many notifications, I want to sort my notification list by type or by reason so that related notifications are grouped together and I can work through them in order.

### User Scenario

I have review requests, assignments and mentions. I sort by reason, then use #50's filter and #51's bulk "Mark as read", and the sort stays the whole time as I mark all the notifications where people have mentioned me as read.

### Acceptance Criteria

_To be written: at least 3 testable criteria, e.g. sort order by type, sort order by reason, sort choice kept in the URL alongside #50's filters._

### Out of Scope

_To be written._

### Open Questions

- **Reason is in scope.** Reason means *why* the user was notified: review requested, mentioned, assigned, or subscribed (watching). Type is *what* the notification is about: issue, pull request, commit or repository. Notifications don't store a reason today: `models/activities/notification.go` → `Notification` has `Source` (the type) but no reason. So this needs a new column and a migration. The reason also has to be passed from the event handlers in `services/uinotification/notify.go` (`PullRequestReviewRequest`, `IssueChangeAssignee`, the `mentions` lists) through the notification queue into `CreateOrUpdateIssueNotifications`.
- Notifications are one row per issue per user, updated on each new event. Which reason wins when the events differ: the latest, or the highest priority (e.g. review requested outranks subscribed)?
- What reason do existing rows get after the migration (e.g. "subscribed" as the default)?
- What is the default sort, and does it change when #50's filters are active?

### Design Decision

_To be written once the approach is chosen (Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences)._

### Scope

medium. The reason set is kept to four values (review requested, mentioned, assigned, subscribed) to stay medium. More GitHub-style reasons (author, commented, state change) can follow in a later issue.

=== #109 Move the "…" row menus on the Actions, Projects and Packages pages to <aria-menu>, with disabled items | author: Jack-Donohue | milestone: Sprint 2 | comments: 1
### User Story

As a keyboard or screen reader user managing a repository, I want the "…" menus on workflow runs, workflows, project columns and package cleanup rules to be operable from the keyboard, so that I can cancel a run, disable a workflow or edit a column without a mouse.

### User Scenario

A maintainer using a screen reader opens the Actions tab. They Tab to a running job's "…" button and hear "More operations, menu button, collapsed". They press Enter, arrow to "Cancel" and press Enter, and the run is cancelled. They open the workflow's "…" menu, where "Disable workflow" is announced as "dimmed" because the workflow is required, so pressing Enter on it does nothing. On a project board they open a column's "…" menu and choose "Edit", and the edit dialog opens.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given the Actions tab, when it renders, then the workflow "…" menu (`templates/repo/actions/list.tmpl`) and every run row's "…" menu (`templates/repo/actions/runs_list.tmpl`) are `<aria-menu>` elements with no `ui dropdown` class, and each trigger is named "More operations".
- [ ] AC2: Given a project board and a user with write access, when it renders, then each column's "…" menu (`templates/projects/view.tmpl`) is an `<aria-menu>`. Edit opens the column modal, and "Set as default" and "Delete" show their confirmation dialogs, by keyboard and by mouse.
- [ ] AC3: Given a package cleanup rule list, when it renders, then each rule's "…" menu (`templates/package/shared/cleanup_rules/list.tmpl`) is an `<aria-menu>`, and "Edit" and "Preview" navigate.
- [ ] AC4: Given a menu item with the `disabled` class, when the menu is open, then the item has `aria-disabled="true"`, arrow keys still reach it, and Enter, Space or a click on it does nothing and leaves the menu open.
- [ ] AC5: Given a required workflow, when its "…" menu is opened, then "Disable workflow" is disabled as in AC4. For a workflow that isn't required, it sends the same enable/disable request as today.
- [ ] AC6: Given each migrated menu, when operated by keyboard, then Enter/Space/ArrowDown opens it with focus on the first item, Home/End and the arrows move focus, and Escape closes it and returns focus to the trigger.
- [ ] AC7: Given a project board, when a column's "…" menu is opened or used by keyboard, then the column is not picked up or moved by the board's drag-and-drop. The menu sits inside `.project-column-header`, which `web_src/js/features/repo-projects.ts` uses as the Sortable drag handle.
- [ ] AC8: A Vitest test in `web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.test.ts` covers AC4. Playwright tests cover cancelling a run and opening a column's Edit dialog by keyboard. The existing suites still pass.

### Out of Scope

- The "Create new runner" menu (`templates/shared/actions/runner_list.tmpl`): it holds a text input and a copy button, so it is a popup, not a menu.
- The Actions page filter menus (actor, status, branch): they show a current selection, so they stay Fomantic like the other filters.
- The run page's own re-run menu in `web_src/js/components/RepoActionView.vue`.

### Open Questions

- Should a disabled item also say *why* it is disabled (for example "required by organisation settings")? (Proposed: not in this issue. Today the menu shows no reason either.)

=== #101 Subscribe to private repository calendar feeds with a revocable calendar token | author: vvchopra | milestone:  | comments: 0
### User Story

Labels: `enhancement`, `scope: medium` · Type: Feature · Part of #36 · Depends on B

## User Story
As a member of a private repository, I want a calendar subscription URL that works without
signing in but only exposes calendar data and can be revoked, so that I can follow private
deadlines in my calendar app without pasting a full-power access token into a third-party service.

### User Scenario

Lena works on the private repo `acme/backend`. On its milestones page she clicks "Subscribe
(iCal)". A dialog explains that the URL contains a personal calendar token and shows
`https://gitea.example/acme/backend/milestones.ics?token=cal_…`. She adds it to Outlook. Later she
pastes the URL by mistake into a shared calendar. She goes to **Settings → Applications →
Calendar token** and clicks "Regenerate", and the old URL stops working at once. When she leaves
the `acme` organization, her feed stops returning `acme/backend` events on its next fetch.


### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given a signed-in user, when they open **Settings → Applications**, then they can
  create, view, regenerate or delete one calendar token. Only a hash is stored, and the plain
  token is shown once, when it is created.
- [ ] AC2: Given a valid calendar token in the `token` query parameter, when it is sent to an
  `.ics` route of a private repo the token owner can read, then the feed is returned with
  `Cache-Control: private`.
- [ ] AC3: Given the same calendar token, when it is sent to any non-`.ics` route (an
  API endpoint, an RSS feed, or a repo page), then it does not authenticate the request.
- [ ] AC4: Given a personal access token, when it is sent as `?token=` to an `.ics` route, then
  it is rejected. Personal access tokens never authenticate calendar feeds.
- [ ] AC5: Given a token whose owner has lost read access to the repository, when the feed is
  fetched, then it returns `404`. Access is checked on every request, not when the token is
  created.
- [ ] AC6: Given a token that has been regenerated or deleted, when the old URL is fetched, then
  it returns `404`.

### Out of Scope

- Tokens limited to one repository, or tokens with expiry dates (possible follow-ups).
- The cross-repository user feed (issue D).
- Admin pages that list or revoke other users' calendar tokens.

### Open Questions

- Should a bad token return `401` or `404`? (Proposed: `404`, so the response does not reveal that
  a private repo exists.)
- Should the token be removed automatically when the user's account is disabled? (Proposed: yes,
  in the same place access tokens are removed.)

### Design Decision

**Decision:** Add a new `calendar_token` table with one row per user: `uid` (unique),
`token_hash`, `token_salt`, `token_last_eight` and `created_unix`. Add a migration and settings
UI. The `.ics` handlers authenticate `?token=` only against this table, then run the normal repo
permission check as that user on every request.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Reuse personal access tokens with a new calendar scope.* Existing RSS feeds already accept
  tokens through `checkRepoFeedTokenScope`. But a PAT is a general credential: a mis-scoped or
  reused one pasted into Google Calendar would leak far more than dates, and #36 rules this out
  explicitly.
- *Use one secret URL per repository (a token stored on the repo).* Thi
=== #102 Subscribe to one personal deadline feed across all my repositories | author: vvchopra | milestone:  | comments: 0
### User Story

Labels: `enhancement`, `scope: small` · Type: Feature · Part of #36 · Depends on C

## User Story
As a developer who works across several repositories, I want a single calendar feed of the
deadlines on issues assigned to me and the milestones in my repositories, so that I subscribe
once instead of once per repository.

### User Scenario

Sam is assigned issues in five repositories. Under **Settings → Applications → Calendar token**
he copies the "All my deadlines" URL, `/sam/deadlines.ics?token=cal_…`, and adds it to his
calendar. His assigned issue deadlines from all five repos show up with the repo name in each
title. When he is unassigned from one issue, it drops off the feed on the next refresh.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given a valid calendar token for user `sam`, when `/sam/deadlines.ics?token=…` is
  fetched, then it returns one VEVENT for each open issue with a deadline assigned to `sam` in a
  repository he can read, with titles prefixed by `owner/repo`.
- [ ] AC2: Given a token that belongs to a different user, or no token, when
  `/sam/deadlines.ics` is fetched, then it returns `404`.
- [ ] AC3: Given that Sam loses access to a repository, when the feed is fetched again, then that
  repository's issues are no longer in it.
- [ ] AC4: Given an issue that also appears in that repository's own `issues.ics`, when both
  feeds are compared, then the event has the same `UID` in both, so a client subscribed to both
  feeds shows it once.
- [ ] AC5: Given more matching issues than the cap from issue B, when the feed is fetched, then
  it returns at most the cap.

### Out of Scope

- A cross-repository in-app `/calendar` page (follow-up once A ships).
- Including issues the user created or is watching but is not assigned to.

### Open Questions

- Should milestones of every repository the user can write to be included, or only issues
  assigned to them? (Proposed: assigned issues only, to keep the query bounded.)


### Design Decision

**Decision:** Build the feed from one `IssuesOptions` query with `AssigneeID = user`, the #34
`HasDeadline` filter and the repository access condition the user dashboard already uses. Render
it with the serializer from issue B, so UIDs match the per-repo feeds.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *Merge the per-repo feeds in Go.* This makes one query per repository, which is slow for users
  in many repos, and it is hard to cap the total size.
- *Let the client subscribe to each repo feed (do nothing).* This is the current pain point for
  users in many repos, and there would be nowhere to put the cross-repo `/calendar` page later.

**Rationale:** A single query bounded by the access condition is cheap and correct when access
changes, and reusing B's serializer keeps the UID scheme in one place.

**Consequences:** The feed depends on the dashboard's access condition staying correct for
private repos and organizations. A later cross-repo `/calendar` page could reuse the same query.

### Scope

small

=== #37 Expedite integration test suite | author: arjunsb26 | milestone:  | comments: 0
### What problem would this solve?

**Summary**
The integration suite takes roughly 25–30 minutes for a full pass, so in practice almost nobody runs it before pushing; contributors push, wait on CI, and find out later. A run on 2026-09-14 consumed the default 10-minute `go test` timeout having completed about 252 of 700 top-level tests. Individual tests run far over the project's own target of sub-2s: thirteen exceeded 10 seconds, and two dominate — `TestActionsScopedWorkflows` at 1m17s and `TestActionsReusableWorkflow` at 50s, both single large blocks whose cost is fixture setup and git I/O rather than assertions. Nothing holds the line today: no budget, no ratchet, and no signal short of the whole CI job timing out.

**User story**
"As a contributor, I want to run the integration tests relevant to my change and get an answer in under a minute so that I can iterate locally instead of using CI as my test runner."

**Rough scope — Large**
Establishing which tests are parallel-safe is itself undocumented groundwork, and the work then spans the test harness, CI configuration, fixture design, and a new enforcement mechanism.

**Source**
Analysis of a full `go test ./...` run of this fork on 2026-09-14, measured against the sub-2s target in `AGENTS.md`.

### What do you propose?

**Solution proposal**
Make the suite something developers actually run:

- **Establish which tests are parallel-safe.** The rule separating tests that tolerate `t.Parallel()` from those needing serial DB state is currently written down nowhere. Document it, then enable parallelism where it is safe. This is groundwork for everything else here.
- **Sharding**, so CI can fan out across N workers and a developer can run a single shard locally.
- **Selective runs** targeting the area you changed, rather than all-or-nothing.
- **An enforced runtime budget.** The test logger already emits `+++ TestX is a slow test (run: …)` lines, so the data exists — turn it into a report, set a per-test ceiling, and fail CI on regressions past it.
- **Faster fixtures for the worst offenders.** Share repository fixtures across subtests in the two Actions tests instead of creating one per `t.Run`, and split them into independently runnable tests. Profile first to confirm setup is the cost rather than the `FlushAll(ctx, 5*time.Second)` calls.
- **Make standard tooling work.** A bare `go test ./...` currently dies at the 10-minute default with a goroutine dump and no failing assertion, because the 40-minute timeout lives only in `Makefile:82`. Either make it work or exit immediately pointing at `make test-integration`. A `testing.Short()` skip would give contributors a fast command that passes.

# Sprint 2 Mid-Sprint Check-in: Carson Rackley (@CarsonRackley)

## What I have done so far, and what remains

I have not completed much implementation yet. Between coursework for other classes, the in-class
presentations and Quiz 2, the first half of the sprint went mostly to planning. I read through the
whole Sprint 2 page and mapped each deliverable to what I owe: two medium issues, a peer-reviewed
spec and at least one design decision with two alternatives per issue, PRs with a Tech Debt
section, AI logs, and UML diagrams. I then updated our shared Claude context files
(`.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`) with the Sprint 2 rules, formats and deadlines, so anyone on
the team can ask Claude which deliverables are still missing.

What remains is most of the sprint's work. I need to choose my two medium issues and put them on
the Sprint 2 milestone, tighten their descriptions and acceptance criteria, and get each spec
peer-reviewed before I write code. Then I implement both with tests, review a teammate's PR, and
draw the class and sequence diagrams (D6) for one of my issues.

## One thing I learned

The biggest thing I learned is how differently Go organizes code compared to the Java I wrote in
Software Dev. Go has no classes. Instead, data is kept in simple structs, and functions are
attached to them separately. Rather than one class inheriting from another, Go builds bigger pieces
by placing one struct inside another, so it reuses that struct's fields and behavior. Interfaces
also work differently: in Java you have to declare that a class implements an interface, but in Go
anything that has the right functions fits automatically. That is how Gitea can use one shared
database helper to look up many different kinds of data. The web pages are built from templates
that the server fills in with data before sending them to the browser. At first this made the code
hard to follow because I kept looking for classes that weren't there. Once I understood the
pattern, tracing my Sprint 1 notification changes through the code became much easier, and I feel
more confident jumping into unfamiliar parts of the codebase.

## One thing I would do differently

I would start earlier. I let this sprint's work get pushed behind other deadlines, so now most of
it lands in the second week, along with the stress of knowing it is still waiting. Even small steps
in the first few days, like picking my issues and posting their specs, would have helped, because
peer review needs turnaround time that I cannot compress at the end. Going forward I plan to set
aside time early in each sprint just for getting my issues set up.

For the project itself, I would be more exploratory when choosing and sizing issues. Before
committing to one, I want to trace the code it touches first (models, routes, templates and tests)
so I know whether it needs a migration or spans several layers. That gives a more honest estimate,
keeps an issue from turning out bigger than it looked, and means I understand the whole
implementation before I start coding instead of discovering it halfway through.

You have about 3½ days left. Sprint 2 closes **Thursday Oct 29, 11:59 PM**, and each spec needs a teammate's `Spec reviewed` comment before you start coding. So whatever you pick, post the specs today and ask for reviews.

## Realistic options (unassigned, or already yours)

**1. #52 Sort notifications by reason or type (medium, assigned to you).** This is effectively required. It's your Sprint 1 stretch goal and it carried over, and the course rule is that unfinished Sprint 1 issues go into the backlog before new work. If you skip it, you have to write the reason on the issue.
- **Pro:** It continues your #50/#51 code, so you already know the area.
- **Con:** The spec is still a skeleton with no ACs, no Out of Scope and no Design Decision. Sorting by *reason* also needs a new column, a migration, and the reason passed from `services/uinotification` through the queue. That's a real medium.
- **To make it faster:** Narrow it to sort by *type* (`Source`, which already exists) plus sort direction, and split "reason" into a follow-up issue. If you keep reason in, your D3 design decision is already there: which reason wins, latest or highest priority.
- **Flag:** You wrote this issue yourself. Normally I'd point that out, but the carryover rule seems to override it here. Ask the TA if you're unsure.
- It isn't on the Sprint 2 milestone yet. Add it for D1.

**2. #109 Move the "…" row menus on the Actions, Projects and Packages pages to `<aria-menu>` (medium, Sprint 2 milestone, unassigned).** This is the most ready-to-go issue on the board.
- **Pro:** The full spec is written (8 ACs, out of scope, open questions). The `<aria-menu>` web component is already on main (`web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.ts`, with Vitest and e2e tests), and Jack is doing the matching #108 and #110, so you have a pattern to follow.
- **Con:** It's mostly template and TypeScript work. AC4 (disabled items) means changing the component itself, and AC7 (don't trigger the project-board drag-and-drop) is fiddly.
- **Flag:** D2 (the spec) is graded individually, and Jack wrote this one. If you take it, rework the spec into your own words and write your own Design Decision. Check with Jack first, since he may have planned it for someone else.

**3. #101 Calendar token for private repo feeds (medium by its body, but no label).**
- I'd avoid this one. It says "Depends on B", which is #100, Vishav's issue, and that's still open. It also needs a new table, a migration, auth handling and a settings UI. That's too much risk for 3 days.

**4. Write a new notifications issue off #7.** #7's original ask includes "save important ones", and nobody has an issue for that. A "Save/star a notification" issue fits naturally next to #52. But you'd be writing a spec from scratch, getting it reviewed and then building it, which is the slowest path.

## My recommendation

#98 Show milestone and issue deadlines in a repository calendar view | author vvchopra | enhancement, | ms: 
### User Story

Labels: `enhancement`, `scope: medium` · Type: Feature · Part of #36
## User Story
As a developer on a repository, I want a month calendar of its milestone due dates and issue
deadlines so that I can see what is due when without scanning the issue list.

### User Scenario

## User Scenario
Priya opens `octo/app` and clicks the new **Calendar** link in the Issues area. She lands on
`/octo/app/calendar`, which shows the current month as a grid. The "Sprint 3" milestone appears on
the 14th, and four issues with deadlines appear on their due days. Each entry shows its title and
links to the milestone or issue. She picks the "Sprint 3" milestone and "assigned to me" in the
filters, and the grid now shows only her Sprint 3 issues. She clicks the next-month arrow, and the
URL updates so she can share that view.

### Acceptance Criteria

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a repository with issues enabled, when a user with read access to issues opens
  `/{owner}/{repo}/calendar`, then a month grid for the current month is shown, with every open
  milestone that has a due date and every issue with a deadline in that month on its due day.
- [ ] AC2: Given an entry on the calendar, when the user clicks it, then they go to that issue or
  milestone page.
- [ ] AC3: Given a milestone, assignee or state (open/closed/all) filter is chosen, when the
  calendar reloads, then only matching issues are shown and the filter values are kept in the
  URL query.
- [ ] AC4: Given the user moves to the previous or next month, when the page reloads, then entries
  for that month are shown and the month is in the URL (`?month=YYYY-MM`).
- [ ] AC5: Given a user without read access to the repository's issues, when they open the
  calendar URL, then they get the same 404 response the issue list gives them.
- [ ] AC6: Given an issue with no deadline (`deadline_unix = 0`), when the calendar is shown, then
  that issue does not appear.

### Out of Scope

## Out of Scope
- `.ics` subscription feeds (issue B, issue C).
- The cross-repository `/calendar` page for the signed-in user (issue D).
- Dragging entries to change a deadline, and week or day views.

### Open Questions

## Open Questions
- Should pull requests that have deadlines appear too, or only issues? (Proposed: issues only, to match #36.)
- Where should the Calendar link go: in the issue list header next to Milestones, or as its own
  repository tab?

### Design Decision

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Render the month grid on the server with a Go template. The handler queries the
month's range with the deadline bounds from #34, and month navigation and filters are plain links
and GET forms.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- *A Vue component that fetches JSON* (the approach #36 suggests, next to `RepoIssuesChart.vue`).
  It would need a new JSON endpoint and client-side date handling. Nothing on this page needs to
  be reactive, and `docs/frontend-vue-components.md` says to use Vue only when the page needs it.
- *An existing JS calendar library (for example FullCalendar).* It adds a large frontend
  dependency and its own styling that would have to match Fomantic and the `tw-` theme colours.

**Rationale:** A server-rendered grid reuses `IssuesOptions` and the filter parsing #34 already
tested. It needs no new endpoint, works without JS, and keeps the whole feature in one layer.

**Consequences:** Every month change reloads the page. Adding interactive features later (drag to
reschedule, hover previews) would mean moving to Vue then. The month boundaries must use
`setting.DefaultUILocation`, matching how #34 pins deadlines to the end of the day.


### Scope

medium
--- vvchopra: # Repository calendar view: design (#98)

Part of #36. Issue: https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/issues/98

## Goal

A month calendar at `/{owner}/{repo}/calendar` showing the repository's open milestone due dates
and the deadlines of its issues **and pull requests**, so users can see what is due when without
scanning the lists. Server-rendered, no JS required.

## Decisions taken during brainstorming

| Question | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Include pull requests? | Yes. Issues and PRs both appear, styled by kind and state. |
| Where is the entry point? | A `Calendar` button next to Milestones in the list header (`templates/repo/issue/list.tmpl`), so it shows on both the Issues and Pull Requests lists. No new repo tab. |
| Milestone entries under filters | They follow the milestone filter (only the selected milestone is shown). Assignee and state filters do not hide milestones. Milestones are always open-only. |
| Busy days | A cell shows 3 entries; the rest sit in a native `<details>` ("+N more") that expands in place. |
| Structure | A new handler plus a pure `buildMonthGrid` function (not reusing `prepareIssueFilterAndList`, not Vue). |

## Changes to the issue body

- Open Questions: answered as in the table above.
- AC1: "every issue **and pull request** with a deadline in that month".
- AC5: 404 only when the user can read **neither** issues nor pull requests; when they can read
  one unit, only that unit's entries appear.
- New AC7: given a day with more than 3 entries, the cell shows 3 and a "+N more" control that
  reveals the rest on the same page.
- Consequences: old milestones store "no due date" as `253370764800` and are skipped; the query is
  capped at 1,000 entries with a visible notice.

## Route

`m.Get("/calendar", repo.Calendar)` in the existing group in `routers/web/web.go` that already holds
`/labels`, `/milestones` and `/milestone/{id}`. That group applies `optSignIn`,
`context.RepoAssignment` and `reqRepoIssuesOrPullsReader`, which gives AC5 with no new guard.

## Query parameters

| Param | Meaning | Missing or invalid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `month` | `YYYY-MM`, year 1970–9998 | current month in `setting.DefaultUILocation`, no error |
| `milestone` | milestone ID in this repo | no milestone filter |
| `assignee` | user ID | no assignee filter |
| `state` | `open`, `closed`, `all` | `open` |

Every navigation and filter link carries the whole query string, so month and filters persist
(AC3, AC4). The prev and next month links come from `calendarMonthLink`, which returns "" at the
1970 and 9998 bounds (where `parseCalendarMonth` would fall back to today); the template hides a
link whose value is empty.

## Handler: `routers/web/repo/calendar.go`

1. `parseCalendarMonth(ctx.FormString("month"), now)` returns the first instant of the month in
   `setting.DefaultUILocation`. `end` is the last second of the month's final day.
2. Pick `IsPull` from unit permissions: both readable → `None`; issues only → `Some(false)`;
   pull requests only → `Some(true)`. An external issue tracker counts as issues not readable.
3. One `issues_model.Issues(ctx, &IssuesOptions{...})` call:
   `RepoIDs = [repo.ID]`, `DeadlineAfterUnix = start`, `DeadlineBeforeUnix = end`,
   `HasDeadline = Some(true)` (AC6), `MilestoneIDs`, `AssigneeID`, `IsClosed`, `IsPull`,
   `SortType: "oldest"`, `Paginator` capped at 1,000. (The `nearduedate` sort prefers a
   milestone's deadline over the issue's own, so it would truncate the wrong rows; cells re-sort by
   deadline in Go anyway.) `Issues` loads each PR through `LoadAttributes`, so there is no separate
   `LoadPullRequests` call. The query asks for `PageSize: calendarMaxEntries + 1`; the extra row only
   detects truncation and is dropped, and `ctx.Data["CalendarTruncated"]` is set when it is present.
   A negative `?milestone` other than -1 ("no milestone") is normalised to 0, so the issue and
   milestone filters agree.
4. Milestones: `db.Find[issues_model.Milestone](ctx, FindMilestoneOptions{RepoID})` with no
   `IsClosed` filter, because the dropdown needs the closed milestones too. `calendarMilestones` then
   keeps the open ones in Go, with `0 < DeadlineUnix < 253370764800` and inside `[start, end]`. With
   a milestone filter, keep only that milestone (`-1` keeps none).
5. Convert issues and milestones to `calendarEntry` values, then
   `ctx.Data["Weeks"] = buildMonthGrid(start, now, entries)`.
6. Fill the milestone and assignee dropdowns with the helpers the issue list already uses.
7. Render `repo/calendar`.

### Grid builder (no side effects, no DB)

```go
type calendarEntry struct {
        Kind  string // "milestone" | "issue" | "pull"
        State string // "open" | "closed" | "merged"
        Index int64  // 0 for milestones
        Title string
        Link  string
        unix  int64 // the deadline, places and orders the entry
}

type calendarDay struct {
        Date    time.Time
        InMonth bool
        IsToday bool
        Entries []calendarEntry
}

func (d calendarDay) Visible() []calendarEntry  // first 3 entries
func (d calendarDay) Overflow() []calendarEntry // the rest, behind "+N more"

func buildMonthGrid(monthStart, now time.Time, entries []calendarEntry) [][]calendarDay
```

- Weeks start on Monday (ISO 8601, as #34's `week` filter). The grid holds whole weeks, padding
  with days from the neighbouring months marked `InMonth=false`.
- Day boundaries come from `time.Date(y, m, d, ..., loc)`, never from adding `24h`, so DST
  transitions cannot shift a date.
- An entry lands on the date of its deadline in `monthStart.Location()`. Deadlines are pinned to
  23:59:59 so they never spill into the next day.
- Inside a cell: milestones first, then issues and PRs by deadline, then by index.

## Template: `templates/repo/calendar.tmpl`

```
repo/header
.ui.container
  .list-header.flex-text-block
    ‹ prev · "October 2026" · next › · Today
    .list-header-filters: Milestone ▾  Assignee ▾   (the issue list's filter_item_* partials)
    State menu (Open · Closed · All), role="group" with an aria-label
  [truncated notice when CalendarTruncated]
  .repo-calendar-grid
    7 weekday header cells (Mon … Sun)
    .repo-calendar-day [.is-other-month] [.is-today]
      <time datetime="YYYY-MM-DD"> weekday label (narrow screens) + day number </time>
      first 3 entries
      <details><summary>+N more</summary> remaining entries </details>
  [empty-month message when the month has no entries]
```

The per-day weekday label is hidden on wide screens, where the header row names the columns, and
shown under 768px, where the grid collapses to an agenda list. The empty-month message is
`repo.calendar.empty`.

Each entry is an `<a>` to its issue, PR or milestone (AC2) with an icon, `#index` for issues and
PRs, and the title truncated with `tw-truncate`; the full title is in `title=`, prefixed with the
state word ("Closed: " or "Merged: ") for closed issues and PRs and merged PRs, since the icon colour
alone does not say it.

| Kind | Icon | Accent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milestone | `octicon-milestone` | `--color-text`, bold title |
| Issue | `octicon-issue-opened` / `octicon-issue-closed` | `--color-green` open, `--color-red` closed |
| Pull request | `octicon-git-pull-request` / `-merged` / `-closed` | `--color-green` open, `--color-purple` merged, `--color-red` closed |

Entry point: a `Calendar` button after the Milestones button in `templates/repo/issue/list.tmpl`.

## CSS: `web_src/css/features/calendar.css`

Imported from `web_src/css/index.css`.

- `.repo-calendar-grid`: CSS grid, `repeat(7, minmax(0, 1fr))`; day cells at least `7rem` tall.
- `.is-other-month`: `--color-text-light-3` text on `--color-box-header`. `.is-today`: a
  `--color-primary` outline.
- Under 768px wide: one column, out-of-month and empty days hidden, so it reads as an agenda list.
  CSS only.
- Use `flex-*` helpers for layout inside cells, not per-child margins.

## Locale

Keys in `options/locale/locale_en-US.json` only: `repo.calendar`, `repo.calendar.today`,
`repo.calendar.prev_month`, `repo.calendar.next_month`, `repo.calendar.more` (`+%d more`),
`repo.calendar.truncated`, `repo.calendar.state`, `repo.calendar.state_all`,
`repo.calendar.empty` ("Nothing is due this month."), plus
`repo.calendar.month_1`…`month_12` and `repo.calendar.weekday_mon`…`weekday_sun`. The locale has no
month or weekday names, and the existing date helpers only render whole dates, so the names are
added as keys. Both families are built with `printf` / `print` in `templates/repo/calendar.tmpl`, so
a grep for the full key finds no use; see `.claude-students/docs/i18n.md`.

## Edge cases

| Case | Handling |
| --- | --- |
| Invalid or out-of-range `?month=` | Current month, no error |
| Milestone with `DeadlineUnix` of `0` or `253370764800` | Not shown |
| DST change inside the month | Correct dates, via `time.Date` boundaries |
| `?milestone=` from another repo | Matches nothing; empty grid, no leak |
| More than 1,000 issues and PRs in the month | First 1,000 by creation date, plus a notice suggesting filters |
| Issues disabled, pull requests enabled | Page allowed; PRs and milestones shown |

## Testing

1. `routers/web/repo/calendar_test.go`, no DB:
   - `TestParseCalendarMonth`: valid values, invalid values and the year bounds.
   - `TestCalendarEntries`: kind and state of issues, PRs (open, closed, merged) and milestones.
   - `TestBuildMonthGrid`: grid shape (Oct 2026 starts Thursday, Feb 2027 fills four rows, Nov 2026
     with DST ending on the 1st), entries on their deadline's day with milestones first, the cell
     limit split, `IsToday` in the grid's location, trailing out-of-month cells, `Visible` and
     `Overflow` edges, and ordering by title on equal deadlines.
   - `TestCalendarIsPull`, `TestCalendarMilestones` and `TestCalendarMonthLink`: the helpers.
2. `TestCalendarHandler` in the same file, with `contexttest.MockContext` and fixtures: an issue
   shows only in its deadline's month, the state and assignee filters, a milestone on its due day,
   unit permissions limiting what shows, and PRs appearing with `Kind == "pull"`.
3. `tests/integration/repo_calendar_test.go`, `TestRepoCalendar`, aiming for under 2 seconds: issues
   and PRs on their days, month navigation keeping the filters, the issue list linking to the
   calendar, and anonymous access (200 on a public repo, 404 on a private one).

No Playwright test: the page has no JS behaviour. Some Go tests fail on native Windows, so run the
integration test on WSL2 or CI.

## Out of scope

`.ics` feeds (#B and #C), the cross-repository `/calendar` page (#D), drag to reschedule, week and
day views, and an exact-date `due=` filter on the issue list.

## How a spec review works here

From `.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md` and the issue templates:

1. **Read the whole spec in the issue body.** D2 grades the spec in the issue body, so review the body, not side comments.
2. **Check it against the course format:**
   - **User Story:** "As a… I want… so that…", and it meets INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
   - **User Scenario:** a concrete walk-through of who does what in the UI.
   - **Acceptance Criteria:** at least 3, each Given/When/Then with a clear pass/fail result.
   - **Out of Scope** and **Open Questions** are filled in ("None" is fine for Open Questions).
   - **Design Decision (D3):** Decision, at least 2 concrete Alternatives Considered and why each lost, Rationale, Consequences. This is graded strictly.
   - **Scope:** stated, with a matching `scope:` label. Also check that the issue is on the Sprint 2 milestone and has exactly one assignee.
3. **Sanity-check it against the code if you can.** For example, confirm that the route group or model it names actually exists.
4. **Post a comment on the issue** that starts with `Spec reviewed — <notes>`. Make the notes substantive: what's good, what's missing, what to change. If there are real gaps, send it back the way #35 was in Sprint 1 ("Spec reviewed — not yet: …"). Vishav revises, and you post a second comment approving it. Vishav can't start coding until you approve.

## Things to check on #98

Do your own read first and confirm these yourself. These are just places to look:

- **The body and the follow-up design comment disagree.** Vishav's comment adds pull requests, rewrites AC5 (404 only when neither issues nor PRs are readable), adds a new AC7 ("+N more" on busy days) and answers both Open Questions. The body still says "issues only" and still lists those questions as open. The body should be updated, since that's what gets graded.
- **AC3 is ambiguous next to the comment.** The comment says assignee and state filters don't hide milestones, but AC3 doesn't say that.
- **Labels and milestone:** the only label is `enhancement` (no `scope: medium`), and the issue isn't on the Sprint 2 milestone. That costs D1 points for the team.
- **Formatting:** every section heading is duplicated (`### User Story` and then `## User Story`), left over from pasting into the template.
- **Is it still medium?** With PRs, per-unit permissions, a 1,000-entry cap, the mobile agenda layout and around 30 locale keys added, it's worth asking whether it has grown toward large, or whether some of that should be split off.
- **What's solid:** the ACs are testable Given/When/Then, and the Design Decision has two real alternatives (a Vue component, or FullCalendar) with reasons. That should satisfy D3. It depends on #34, which is closed, so that's fine.

Write the comment yourself. A copied AI review is the kind of thing the Honor Code rules flag. If you used this session to prepare, say so in an AI Assistance comment with role "Other (spec review)" once you've run `specstory sync` and filed the log.

=== #117 Group notifications by repository | labels: enhancement,scope: medium, | ms: Sprint 2 | assignees: CarsonRackley,
Part of #7. Builds on #50 (filter by repository and type) and #51 (bulk actions). Upstream request: go-gitea/gitea#9605.

### User Story

As a user who gets notifications from many repositories, I want to group my notification list by repository so that I can work through one project at a time without filtering to each repository in turn.

### User Scenario

Priya has 45 unread notifications spread across `org/backend`, `org/frontend` and `org/docs`. On the Notifications page she picks "Group by repository". The list turns into one section per repository, each headed by the repository name and its unread count, with that repository's notifications newest first. She collapses `org/docs` to deal with it later, works through `org/backend`, and marks its rows read with the bulk bar from #51. The grouping stays on as the list refreshes and when she moves to page 2, and the URL keeps it, so her bookmark opens the grouped view next time.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given notifications from at least two repositories, when the user selects "Group by repository", then the list shows one section per repository, each headed by the repository's full name and its unread notification count, with the section's rows ordered newest first.
- [ ] AC2: Given grouping is on, when the list loads, then the sections are ordered by repository full name A–Z, and the order does not change when a new notification arrives and the list refreshes.
- [ ] AC3: Given grouping is on and there are more notifications than fit on one page, when the user moves between pages, then every repository's notifications are contiguous, and a section that continues from the previous page repeats its header marked "(continued)".
- [ ] AC4: Given grouping is on, when the user switches between the Unread and Read tabs, changes the #50 repository or type filter, pages, marks a single notification read or pinned, or runs a #51 bulk action, then grouping is still on afterwards (`group=repo` is kept in the URL), and the in-place list refresh keeps it too.
- [ ] AC5: Given grouping is on, when the user activates a section header with the mouse, Enter or Space, then that section collapses or expands, and screen readers announce whether it is expanded.
- [ ] AC6: Given a pinned notification, when grouping is on, then it is listed inside its repository's section with its pin icon, not in a separate section.
- [ ] AC7: Given grouping is off (the default), when the page loads, then the list looks and behaves exactly as it does today: newest first, no section headers.

### Out of Scope

- Grouping by type or by reason. Reason needs a schema change and stays in #52.
- Per-section actions, such as "Mark this repository as read". The #50 repository filter plus "Mark all as read" already covers this.
- Remembering the grouping choice or collapsed sections between visits, other than through the URL.
- Changes to the notifications API (`/api/v1/notifications`).

### Open Questions

- Should the section header link to the repository? (Proposed: yes, the name is a link and the rest of the header toggles the section.)
- Should "Select page" in the bulk bar also get a per-section checkbox? (Proposed: no for this issue; selection stays per row and per page as in #51.)

### Design Decisions

#### Decision 1: Order grouped notifications by repository in the query, not on the page

**Decision:** When grouping is on, the list query sorts by repository full name and then newest first, and pagination stays at 20 rows per page.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Keep the newest-first query and group only the 20 rows already on the page. This is simplest, but one repository shows up on every page in a different spot, which defeats grouping. (b) Turn pagination off when grouping is on, so every group is complete on one page. This is unbounded for users with thousands of read notifications.
**Rationale:** Sorting in the query is the only option that keeps each repository together across pages while keeping page size bounded.
**Consequences:** The notification find options need a sort option, because the order is fixed to `updated_unix DESC` today, and the sort needs a join on the repository. A group can be split across a page boundary, which AC3's "(continued)" header handles.

#### Decision 2: Sections are ordered A–Z, not by most recent activity

**Decision:** Repository sections are ordered alphabetically by full name.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Order sections by each repository's newest notification, like the ungrouped list. (b) Order by unread count, highest first.
**Rationale:** The list refreshes in place whenever the unread count changes, so with (a) or (b) the sections would jump around while the user is reading or selecting rows. Alphabetical order stays put, and the user can find a repository where they expect it.
**Consequences:** A busy repository late in the alphabet can sit on page 2 or later. The #50 repository filter is the way to jump straight to it.

#### Decision 3: The grouping choice lives in the URL, like the #50 filters

**Decision:** Grouping is a `group=repo` query parameter, carried through every link, form and refresh the filters already carry.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Save it as a per-user setting on the server. (b) Save it in the browser's local storage.
**Rationale:** It matches #50's decision that filters live in the URL: bookmarkable, shareable, and it comes back clean when the user leaves the page. A server setting adds a settings page entry and a write on every toggle for a view preference. Local storage would be invisible to the server-rendered page and the `div-only` refresh.
**Consequences:** Every place that rebuilds the notifications URL (tab links, filter links, pagination, single-row status actions, bulk actions, `div-only` refresh, redirects) has to carry `group`, which is the same set of places #50 changed for `repo` and `source`.

### Scope

medium

=== #118 Alert me to new notifications with a tab icon badge and opt-in desktop notifications | labels: enhancement,scope: medium, | ms: Sprint 2 | assignees: CarsonRackley,
Part of #7. Upstream requests: go-gitea/gitea#1415 (badge on the favicon) and go-gitea/gitea#31925 (browser notifications).

### User Story

As a user who keeps Gitea open in a background tab, I want the tab icon to show when I have unread notifications, and optionally a desktop notification when a new one arrives, so that I notice review requests and mentions without switching back to check.

### User Scenario

Marco keeps Gitea open in one of many browser tabs while he codes. On the Notifications page he clicks "Enable desktop notifications", and the browser asks for permission once. He allows it. Later a teammate requests his review. A dot appears on the Gitea tab's icon, and a desktop notification says "You have 1 new notification". He clicks it, and the browser switches to Gitea and opens his notifications. After he reads it, the unread count drops to zero and the dot disappears. When he is already looking at Gitea, no desktop notification pops up; the navbar count is enough.

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given a signed-in user with at least one unread notification, when any Gitea page loads or the unread count updates, then the tab icon shows a badge dot, and when the count drops to 0 the default icon comes back without a reload.
- [ ] AC2: Given an Actions run page, which already sets the tab icon to the run's status, when the user also has unread notifications, then the run status icon is shown, not the notification badge.
- [ ] AC3: Given desktop notifications have never been enabled in this browser, when new notifications arrive, then no desktop notification is shown and the browser never asks for permission on its own.
- [ ] AC4: Given the user clicks "Enable desktop notifications" on the Notifications page, when the browser asks for permission and the user denies it, then the page says notifications are blocked by the browser and the setting stays off.
- [ ] AC5: Given desktop notifications are enabled and permission is granted, when the unread count goes up while the Gitea tab is hidden, then exactly one desktop notification is shown saying how many new notifications there are, without the issue title or repository name.
- [ ] AC6: Given Gitea is open in several tabs, when the unread count goes up, then the user gets one desktop notification, not one per tab.
- [ ] AC7: Given the Gitea tab is visible, or the count stays the same or goes down, when the count updates, then no desktop notification is shown.
- [ ] AC8: Given a desktop notification is shown, when the user clicks it, then the browser focuses Gitea and opens `/notifications`.
- [ ] AC9: Given desktop notifications are enabled, when the user clicks "Disable desktop notifications", then no more desktop notifications are shown in that browser.

### Out of Scope

- Notifications when no Gitea tab is open (Web Push with a service worker and server-side keys).
- A number inside the badge, or a count in the page title.
- Per-type or per-repository rules for which notifications alert.
- Sounds, email, and the mobile or API side of notifications.

### Open Questions

- Should the badge be something the user can turn off? (Proposed: no. It is passive and only appears when there is something unread.)
- Should the alert also fire when the page falls back to polling because the event stream is unavailable? (Proposed: yes, both update paths behave the same.)

### Design Decisions

#### Decision 1: The desktop notification opt-in is stored per browser, not on the account

**Decision:** "Enable desktop notifications" is remembered in the browser's local storage.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A per-user setting stored on the server, shown in Settings. (b) No stored setting: alert whenever the browser permission is granted.
**Rationale:** Browser permission is per browser and per device anyway, and browsers only allow the permission prompt after a click. A server-side setting would turn on in a browser that never granted permission and would have to prompt without a click, which browsers block. With (b), users who granted permission for something else could not turn the alerts off without revoking it.
**Consequences:** No server or schema change. The choice does not follow the user to other browsers, and clearing site data turns it off.

#### Decision 2: The desktop notification shows only a count

**Decision:** The notification text is "You have N new notifications" and clicking it opens `/notifications`.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Show the newest notification's issue title and repository. (b) Show one notification per new item, each linking to its issue.
**Rationale:** The live update only delivers a count, so (a) and (b) need an extra API request per update. Titles from private repositories would also appear on a lock screen or a shared screen. A count is enough to make the user switch tabs.
**Consequences:** The user cannot tell a review request from a subscription update until they open Gitea. Richer content is follow-up work if users ask for it.

#### Decision 3: Badge as a dot, with Actions run status taking precedence

**Decision:** The badge is a plain dot drawn on the Gitea icon, reusing the drawing code that already badges the icon with an Actions run's status. On a run page the run status wins.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Draw the unread number in the icon. (b) Put the count in the page title, like "(3) Gitea".
**Rationale:** A number is unreadable at 16 px and needs a "9+" cap. The title is truncated in a crowded tab bar and changes the text screen readers announce. On a run page the user is watching that run, so its status is the more useful icon.
**Consequences:** The icon code needs to know which badge currently owns the icon, so leaving a run page or reading every notification restores the right one.

### Scope

medium

  const notificationDiv = document.querySelector('#notification_div');
  if (!notificationDiv) return;

  try {
    const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
    params.set('div-only', 'true');
    params.set('sequence-number', String(++notificationSequenceNumber));
    const response = await GET(`${appSubUrl}/notifications?${params.toString()}`);

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error('Failed to fetch notification table');

      notificationDiv.outerHTML = data;
      // the page load already consumed the flash, so the refreshed list would drop e.g. a bulk action's confirmation
      const container = document.querySelector('#notification_div > .ui.container')!;
      if (flash && !container.querySelector('.flash-message')) container.prepend(flash);
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

1. **Collapsed sections re-expand on every refresh.** This is the biggest gap. `updateNotificationTable()` in `web_src/js/features/notification.ts` replaces the whole `#notification_div` (`outerHTML = data`) whenever the count changes. Out of Scope only rules out remembering collapse *between visits*. Add an AC that collapse state survives the in-place refresh, or make it a deliberate limitation. Either way it's a good Design Decision candidate: carry it in the URL, keep it in JS memory and re-apply after refresh, or don't keep it at all.
2. **Collapsed rows and "Select page".** If a section is collapsed, does #51's "Select page" select the hidden rows, so a bulk action hits things the user can't see? Your second Open Question is close to this, but it should answer this case directly.
3. **What does the header count?** AC1 says "its unread notification count".

4. **Sort detail:** Decision 1 sorts by "repository full name". Name the columns (owner name and lower-case repo name) so A–Z is case-insensitive and testable.

## #118 Tab icon badge and opt-in desktop notifications

1. **AC6 (one alert across tabs) has no mechanism behind it, and it conflicts with Open Question 2.**
   - The shared worker sends `notification-count` to *every* connected tab, so each hidden tab would fire its own alert.
   - In polling fallback (no `SharedWorker`/`EventSource`), each tab polls on its own.
   - The usual fix is a fixed Notification `tag`, so the OS replaces duplicates instead of stacking them. Add that as a Decision with alternatives (a `tag`, `BroadcastChannel`/localStorage leader election, or alerting only from the worker), or AC6 isn't really implementable as written.
2. **"Visible" is ambiguous with several tabs.** AC7 says no alert when "the Gitea tab is visible". If one Gitea tab is visible and two are hidden, should the hidden ones still alert? State it.
3. **"N new" vs total unread.** Is N the increase since the last count, or the total unread? The scenario's "1 new notification" fits either. Pick one, since AC5 and the tests depend on it.
4. **Unsupported or insecure context.** The Notification API only works on HTTPS (or localhost), and lots of self-hosted Gitea runs on plain HTTP. Add an AC for what the button does when it's unavailable (hidden, or a message), and one for permission revoked later in browser settings.

33	## What changed and why
34	
35	On GitHub, `c` starts a new issue or pull request from the list, and opens the commit picker on a pull request's changed files. Gitea had no such shortcut. Building on #56's registry and #58's link shortcuts, this PR adds `c` in those three places.
36	
37	- **The create buttons declare `c` themselves.** "New Issue" and "New Pull Request" are links, so they declare `c` the same way #58's tabs declare their `g` shortcuts, and `c` goes where the button leads, exactly as a click would. When the repository uses issue templates, that is the template chooser.
38	- **Only a button that really creates something declares it.** An archived repository has no create button, and its pull request list shows "Compare commits" in that place; a "New Pull Request" button the user can't use is greyed out. The list page already decides all of this, so in each of these cases `c` simply doesn't exist.
39	- **The commit picker declares `c` itself.** It is a Vue component that builds its own button, so it adds `c` when it appears on the "Files changed" tab. `c` opens it as a click does, ending with focus on its first entry. It first moves focus to the picker's button, so Escape and the arrow keys work even while the commits are still loading, and it never closes an open picker.
40	- **Typing into a filter menu no longer runs a shortcut.** Gitea's older dropdowns without a search box jump to the item starting with a typed letter, but didn't mark the key as used, so `c` in the issue list's "Type" filter left for the new issue page instead of picking "Created by you". Gitea's patch for those dropdowns now marks the letter as used, which #56's registry already respects. This helps every shortcut, not only `c`. Only a letter typed on the dropdown itself is marked: typing into a filter box inside a dropdown's menu, such as the Label filter, works as before.
41	- **Each `c` is listed with what it opens** ("New Issue", "New Pull Request" or "Filter by commit"), under "Issues" on the lists and "Pull Requests" on the "Files changed" tab, using existing strings, so nothing new needs translating.
42	- The docs in `.claude-students` describe how a component adds its own shortcut.
43	- Like `s`, `t` and the `g` keys, `c` can't be turned off yet; #60 adds that setting.
44	
45	## How the changes relate to the ACs
46	
47	- **AC1:** `c` on the issue list goes where "New Issue" leads: the new issue page, or the template chooser.
48	- **AC2:** `c` on the pull request list goes where "New Pull Request" leads.
49	- **AC3:** a greyed-out "New Pull Request" button, and an archived repository's lists, declare no `c`, so it does nothing.
50	- **AC4:** on the "Files changed" tab, `c` opens the commit picker with focus on its first entry, and the arrow keys and Escape work as after a click.
51	- **AC5:** `c` only exists on those three pages, so it does nothing elsewhere; when `c` is the second key of `g c`, only `g c` runs.
52	- **AC6:** each `c` is described by what it opens, under "Issues" on the lists and "Pull Requests" on the "Files changed" tab.
53	
54	## How it was tested
55	
56	### Test strategy
57	
58	Almost all of this PR is wiring: which button declares `c` is decided by the list page, and the commit picker only exists on a real pull request. So the tests are Playwright tests on real pages.
59	
60	- **Unit tests for what a page can't show.** Which shortcuts the picker lists isn't visible anywhere until #57's dialog exists, so `web_src/js/components/DiffCommitSelector.test.ts` mounts the picker and checks that it lists `c` as "Filter by commit" in "Pull Requests" (AC6). Whether a dropdown marks a typed letter as used is invisible on a page too, so three tests in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.test.ts` check it directly: a letter typed on a dropdown without a search box is used and Ctrl+C isn't, while typing into a search box, a search box inside the menu, or an input in a menu item is left alone. Everything else is covered by earlier unit tests: #58's for a link turning into a shortcut, and #56's for `c` inside `g c`. Opening the picker is left to Playwright, because a unit test would have to fake the loading of the commits and the focus handling, and would mostly test the fakes.
61	- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** Each of the 6 new tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` sets up the situation where a mistake would show. A signed-in user who can write to the repository, because "New Pull Request" is only usable with write access or a fork; the same repository with an issue template, where "New Issue" leads to the chooser instead. Focus in the "Type" filter, where `c` is also the menu's own letter for "Created by you", and typing into the Label filter, whose search box sits inside its menu and must still take every letter. A signed-out visitor, for whom "New Pull Request" is greyed out, and an archived repository, where "Compare commits" takes its place and shares its `issue-list-new` class. A real pull request's "Files changed" tab, the only place the picker exists and the only way to see where focus lands, once normally and once with its commits held back, since focus only matters while they load.
62	- **What "nothing happens" means here.** For AC3 the tests check that the page declares no `c`, instead of pressing `c` and waiting to see that nothing happened. Showing that a key didn't start a navigation races with whatever is pressed next, and whether `c` exists is decided by the declaration alone.
63	
64	**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked via mutation testing to ensure that the tests actually detect something real: declaring `c` on the greyed-out "New Pull Request" button, declaring it on "Compare commits" in an archived repository, removing it from "New Issue", letting `c` close an open picker, opening it without moving focus to its button first, removing the dropdown fix, and an earlier version of that fix which blocked typing into the Label filter. For the unit tests: dropping the picker's section, changing its description, not registering `c` at all, and for the dropdown, not marking the letter, marking it inside a search box too, marking it with Ctrl, marking a letter typed into an input inside the dropdown, and ignoring a search box inside the menu. Each break failed the matching test, and #56's and #58's tests stayed green.
65	
66	**Not covered automatically, and why.** `c` doing nothing on an issue's own page, the compare page and a pull request's conversation tab was checked by hand, since there is no picker or create button there to declare it.
67	
68	**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance: both lists signed in and out, an archived repository, and a real pull request's "Files changed" tab, where `c` and a mouse click gave the same focus steps through the arrow keys. It also typed into the Label filter on the list and the label picker on an issue, with and without the dropdown fix. I personally spot checked the features to ensure the features work as expected, such as on the issue list, in the filter, and on a pull request's "Files changed" tab.
69	
70	| AC | What the tests check |
71	| --- | --- |
72	| AC1 | On the issue list, `c` goes to the new issue page, and to the template chooser once the repository has an issue template |
73	| AC2 | On the pull request list, `c` goes where "New Pull Request" leads |
74	| AC3 | Signed out, the greyed-out "New Pull Request" declares no `c`; in an archived repository neither list declares `c`, though "Compare commits" is shown |
75	| AC4 | On a real pull request's "Files changed" tab, `c` opens the picker with focus on its first entry, the arrow keys move within it, `c` again leaves it open, and Escape closes it and returns focus to its button, also while its commits are still loading |
76	| AC5 | On the issue list, `g c` goes to the front page instead of starting a new issue; `c` typed into the "Type" filter picks "Created by you" and starts no new issue |
77	| AC6 | "New Issue" and "New Pull Request" are in "Issues"; the mounted picker lists `c` as "Filter by commit" in "Pull Requests" |

function attachDomEvents(dropdown: HTMLElement, focusable: HTMLElement, menu: HTMLElement) {
  // when showing, it has class: ".animating.in"
  // when hiding, it has class: ".visible.animating.out"
  const isMenuVisible = () => (menu.classList.contains('visible') && !menu.classList.contains('out')) || menu.classList.contains('in');

  // update aria attributes according to current active/selected item
  const refreshAriaActiveItem = () => {
    const menuVisible = isMenuVisible();
    focusable.setAttribute('aria-expanded', menuVisible ? 'true' : 'false');

    // if there is an active item, use it (the user is navigating between items)
    // otherwise use the "selected" for combobox (for the last selected item)
    const active = $(menu).find('> .item.active, > .item.selected, > .scrolling.menu > .item.selected')[0];
    if (!active) return;
    // if the popup is visible and has an active/selected item, use its id as aria-activedescendant
    if (menuVisible) {
      focusable.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant', active.id);
    } else if ((dropdown as any)[ariaPatchKey].listPopupRole === 'menu') {
      // for menu, when the popup is hidden, no need to keep the aria-activedescendant, and clear the active/selected item
      focusable.removeAttribute('aria-activedescendant');
      active.classList.remove('active', 'selected');
    }
  };

  dropdown.addEventListener('keydown', (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.isComposing) return;
    // here it must use keydown event before dropdown's keyup handler, otherwise there is no Enter event in our keyup handler
    if (e.key === 'Enter') {
      const elItem = menu.querySelector<HTMLElement>(':scope > .item.selected, .menu > .item.selected');
      // if the selected item is clickable, then trigger the click event.
      // we can not click any item without check, because Fomantic code might also handle the Enter event. that would result in double click.
      if (elItem?.matches('a, .js-aria-clickable') && !elItem.matches('.tw-hidden, .filtered')) {
        e.preventDefault();
        elItem.click();
      }
    }
    // a letter typed on a dropdown without a search box (Fomantic counts one in its menu too) jumps to an item, so it runs no page shortcut

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-26 15:51:04Z)**_

I've reviewed PR #114 from a fetched copy. Your working tree wasn't touched, and I haven't run any tests. The code is solid: one recommended change, a couple of optional notes, and nothing that blocks merging.

## What the PR does

It adds `c` in three places. "New Issue" and "New Pull Request" each declare it on the link itself. The commit picker (`DiffCommitSelector.vue`) registers it when it appears. It also changes `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.ts` so a letter typed on a dropdown with no search box is marked as used and doesn't run a page shortcut.

## What I checked against the code

- **AC3 holds.** The greyed-out New PR button only gets the shortcut attributes inside `{{if .PullRequestCtx.CanCreateNewPull}}`. Archived repos take the `{{else}}` branch ("Compare commits"), which has no `c`.
- **Shortcuts don't fire while typing in a box.** The registry skips events that are already `defaultPrevented` and anything typed in `input, textarea, select` (`web_src/js/modules/shortcut.ts:50`). The dropdown listener runs on the element, before the document-level registry, so marking the key as used there does stop the shortcut.
- **CodeRabbit's "notification repo filter blocked" finding is fixed.** It was raised against your #50 filter. Commit `201d1e4` only marks the key when `e.target === dropdown`. Your filter's markup (`.menu > .ui.search.input > input`) also matches Fomantic's `selector.search` (`'.menu > .search > input'`), so `has search` is true and typing goes into the box.
- **The commit picker opens correctly and stops cleanly.** The action returns early if the menu is already open, and focuses `expandBtn` before `toggleMenu()`, which itself focuses `showAllChanges` after loading. The shortcut goes away with the component through the registry's `element.isConnected` check (`shortcut.ts:17`), so no `unmounted` cleanup is needed.
- **The log change is a rename.** `issue-58-impl.md` was replaced by `issue-58-59-impl.md`, and #58's and #59's AI comments already link the new name on `main`. Those links will work once this merges.

## Findings

1. **Recommended: the dropdown fix swallows more than letters.** Fomantic sends every key that isn't one of its own control keys to `selectedLetter(String.fromCharCode(e.which))` (`dropdown.js:1670`). The new check, `e.key.length === 1 && e.key !== ' '`, therefore marks `?`, digits and punctuation as used too. None of those can ever match an item. Once #115 (`?` help dialog) merges, pressing `?` while a filter dropdown is focused will do nothing. Narrowing the check to letters and digits, e.g. `/^[\p{L}\p{N}]$/u.test(e.key)`, would keep the fix and leave `?` working. A unit test case for `?` would cover it.
2. **Optional: Tech Debt "Introduced: None" understates the dropdown change.** It changes behaviour for every non-search Fomantic dropdown on the site, not just the ones #59 touches. That's worth one sentence under Introduced, or under Design.
3. **Optional: description format.** The course format has separate **What changed** and **Why** sections. ab-wm already declined CodeRabbit's version of this note. It still costs points on the per-PR description score, so mention it as optional and leave it there.

```text
### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] AC1: Given notifications from at least two repositories, when the user selects "Group by repository", then the list shows one section per repository, each headed by the repository's full name and its unread notification count, with the section's rows ordered newest first.
- [ ] AC2: Given grouping is on, when the list loads, then the sections are ordered by repository full name A–Z, and the order does not change when a new notification arrives and the list refreshes.
- [ ] AC3: Given grouping is on and there are more notifications than fit on one page, when the user moves between pages, then every repository's notifications are contiguous, and a section that continues from the previous page repeats its header marked "(continued)".
- [ ] AC4: Given grouping is on, when the user switches between the Unread and Read tabs, changes the #50 repository or type filter, pages, marks a single notification read or pinned, or runs a #51 bulk action, then grouping is still on afterwards (`group=repo` is kept in the URL), and the in-place list refresh keeps it too.
- [ ] AC5: Given grouping is on, when the user activates a section header with the mouse, Enter or Space, then that section collapses or expands, and screen readers announce whether it is expanded.
- [ ] AC6: Given a pinned notification, when grouping is on, then it is listed inside its repository's section with its pin icon, not in a separate section.
- [ ] AC7: Given grouping is off (the default), when the page loads, then the list looks and behaves exactly as it does today: newest first, no section headers.

### Out of Scope

- Grouping by type or by reason. Reason needs a schema change and stays in #52.
- Per-section actions, such as "Mark this repository as read". The #50 repository filter plus "Mark all as read" already covers this.
- Remembering the grouping choice or collapsed sections between visits, other than through the URL.
- Changes to the notifications API (`/api/v1/notifications`).

### Open Questions

- Should the section header link to the repository? (Proposed: yes, the name is a link and the rest of the header toggles the section.)
- Should "Select page" in the bulk bar also get a per-section checkbox? (Proposed: no for this issue; selection stays per row and per page as in #51.)

### Design Decisions
```

	tplNotificationSubscriptions templates.TplName = "user/notification/notification_subscriptions"
